terms.grammar: major (natū) agreeing with frāter; the younger is frāter minor
evidence: Cic. Phil. 11.17: P. Āfricānus, frāter major L. Scīpiōnis
terms.comment: The older brother is frāter major, the younger frāter minor; major natū says outright that the difference is one of age. Terence and Cicero both say frāter major plainly.

phrases.latin: quem meus Cicerō et amābat ut frātrem et jam ut majōrem frātrem verēbātur
phrases.english: whom my Cicero loved as a brother, and already looked up to as a big brother

phrases.latin: senī' nostrī, Dāve, frātrem majōrem Chremem nōstin'?
phrases.english: Davus, do you know Chremes, our old master’s elder brother?

phrases.latin: Frāter tuus major tē exspectat; mātūrā.
phrases.english: Your big brother is waiting for you; hurry up.

sources: The grouped card gave no source for this word.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 24.
